qualifier: This page is for advocates who handle frozen bank account and mule account cases and want a fintech law career alongside their practice.
symptom_title: A frozen account, a desperate client, few answers
symptom: A shopkeeper or a student walks in. Their account is frozen because money from a fraud passed through it, often without their knowledge. Rent is due, wages are stuck, and the branch says only that it has instructions.

You write to the bank, the cyber cell and the court. You know the KYC trail, the freeze request and which officer can actually lift the hold. You have read more bank replies than most fintech founders ever will.
It is real work for people in trouble. But it repeats, it depends on officials who reply slowly, and it never reaches the companies that design these accounts and apps.
outcome_title: From unlocking accounts to advising the apps
outcome: Payment apps, digital lenders and wallets need lawyers who understand KYC and account rules from the inside. They need that knowledge in their user terms, their partner contracts and their compliance work. A user agreement that explains suspensions clearly saves a company, and its users, a great deal of trouble.

A fintech law career lets you do that work with startups and tech companies while your practice continues. It is the same banking knowledge, offered to a payer that builds products instead of a client fighting a freeze.
alternatives_title: Paths that keep you at the same counter

alternatives.t: Becoming the local name for freeze cases
alternatives.why: Referrals grow, but every file still means letters to banks and waiting for the police. The practice gets busier without becoming a fintech career.

alternatives.t: Applying to a fintech legal team with a litigation CV
alternatives.why: Hiring teams look for contracts and compliance work they recognise. A list of freeze matters, however strong, does not show them a document.
Your knowledge grows, but nobody sees it. Without a finished work sample or a way to reach founders, the reading stays private study.

reframe_title: You know where the product breaks
reframe: Most fintech founders understand their app from the code outward. You understand it from the frozen account backward: which check failed, which notice never went out, which clause left the user with no remedy.

That is a positioning advantage, not a gap to fill. Moving into fintech law means presenting that view where it is wanted, in contracts and terms, instead of in another letter to a branch manager. The cases you already handle become your credentials.
cost_title: If the knowledge stays at the branch
cost: Without a move, the same cases keep coming, and your detailed understanding of how accounts work stays known to your clients alone. For a lawyer who sees this much of the system, that is a gentle but real loss.
role_h2: What fintech law work looks like for a lawyer handling frozen account cases
role: Reading a payment app's terms with the user's crisis in mind. Do they explain how the arrangement can end, whether liability is capped, and where the privacy policy sits? Day 3 teaches a six-point terms review that asks exactly this.

Understanding how fintech products are put together. Day 1 explains white labelling, where one company's service carries another's brand, and APIs, which connect an app to a bank. Both come up constantly in fintech contracts.

Seeing how the client makes money. Day 2 covers six business models, including commission and affiliate and marketplace models. Payment and lending apps often earn this way, and each model creates its own contract and compliance work.
first_artifact: After the camp you would have drafted the key clauses of a software development agreement with us on Day 1 and reviewed a startup's terms on Day 3. Applied afterwards to a payment app's terms, the same review draws directly on what your cases taught you. Your notes would read like those of someone who has seen the other end.
longer_term: With 2 hours a day, split between learning and outreach, the next six months could add fintech structuring and fintech compliance, both on the Day 2 plan, to policies and contracts. Outreach starts in the first week, and your freeze practice can carry on through all of it. Each month adds a document you could show a payments founder.

faq.q: Is fintech law only for corporate lawyers?
faq.a: No. It needs people who understand how money and accounts move, and you see that every week. The camp adds the contract and terms side you have not yet practised.

faq.q: Can I reach fintech founders as a practising advocate?
faq.a: Advocates may not advertise or solicit briefs. The approach we teach is relationship building: notice something useful in a public document, share it, and let trust grow. Your State Bar Council can confirm what applies to you.

faq.q: Do I need a finance or technology degree?
faq.a: No. Your LLB and your cases are the base. No coding is needed, because the legal work follows how the business makes money.

faq.q: How much time does this take?
faq.a: Three live evenings, 24 to 26 Oct, then about 2 hours a day: one hour of learning and one hour of outreach and building a track record.

closing_title: Frozen account lawyers: move into fintech law
closing: Lawyers who handle frozen bank account cases already understand KYC and account rules better than most. Payment apps and lenders need that understanding in their contracts and terms. Join three live evenings and build a fintech law career without pausing your practice.
